My name is Daniel, I'm a software engineer by trade, and I start a lot of personal software projects: ranging from simple tools to make my life easier, to complicated microservice-based web applications. What I don't tend to do is follow through and finish them.

Invariably Abandoned is intended to be the story of those projects: why I started them, why I abandoned them, and maybe a little something I learned along the way.

Ready to go

You've created your perfect single-page application, you have your bundler all configured (whether that be vite, create-react-app or some new kid on the block) and you're ready to make it available to the world.

Should you deploy to your favourite object storage (s3, r2, etc), and put your favourite CDN proxy in front of it (Cloudflare, CloudFront etc)?
Or should you consider deploying your SPA with docker?

Usually, the answer is: go ahead with the object storage and proxy and call it a day. This is almost definitely the cheaper option for a small project (free or near-free), will perform great, and will not require you to look after any infrastructure. This approach is also widely documented and there are cookbooks, baked ci jobs and blog posts about it in abundance.

But, there are a few cases where Docker may be the better option for you...

Why Docker

Some reasons you might consider Docker:

  • You want your entire stack (client, API, other resources) to be consolidated in a helm template or docker-compose file.
  • You want to deploy the same build artifact to different environments (maybe staging, ci, and prod) but vary environment variables (traditional SPA tools like vite or create-react-app make this difficult and you're forced to build the application multiple times - one for each environment).
  • You want to be able to deploy your application locally the same as you would in the cloud/production without the inconvenience and complexity that comes with using something like localstack.

First Ideas

Two simple approaches come to mind when thinking about how to get from your SPA source into a ready-for-prod docker container.

Static Container

The first approach would be to build your application either outside the container or using multi-step builds and copy it straight into a proven static web server container (like nginx).

Here's an example Dockerfile:

FROM node:16 as build

ARG VITE_WELCOME_MESSAGE

COPY . .
RUN npm ci
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:1.22.1

COPY --from=build dist /usr/share/nginx/html

// TODO talk about the problem with routing

You have already spotted a potential problem with this... //TODO talk about env variables

For some applications, this can be perfect, but as soon as you have any environment variables (maybe an API URL, a google analytics id or anything else you need to configure) the approach falls over as vite, create-react-app and others need their environment variables at build time, not at run time.

Build on Container Start

What about deploying our source into the docker container and having it built as soon as it starts? Here's an example Dockerfile:

FROM node:16 as node

# Copy everything including our source, package.json and node_modules
COPY . .

# Install the serve npm package
RUN npm i -g serve

# On container start, build the app and serve it
CMD <<EOR
  npm run build
  npx serve ./build
EOR

This solution works 🎉 - and is super simple! Unfortunately, it comes with a downside which is usually a deal-breaker: performance.

Modern tooling tends to use a lot of resources to build a production bundle, in the best case, this means your application takes a very long time to become available - sometimes minutes depending on the hardware (a pain you will feel every time you push an update). And in the worst case where you have a Kubernetes cluster with resource limits, it will result in your container being evicted for being too hungry.

The other problem with this approach is we now have a much larger image size than we need because the full application source and dev dependencies node_modules are included in our docker container.

Best of both worlds

Maybe we can have our cake and eat it too. Let's take our initial static container idea and modify it to allow us to still inject configuration at runtime.

Should you deploy to your favourite object storage (s3, r2, etc), and put your favourite CDN proxy in front of it (Cloudflare, CloudFront etc)?
Or should you consider deploying your SPA with docker?

Pagination using offset/limit is ubiquitous, simple to understand and works excellently in most cases... but you shouldn't use it, at least not visibly.

This article will hopefully convince you of the shortfalls of offset/limit and equip you with some strategies to avoid them.

The offset/limit API

We're going to use an example of a JS project calling a rest api example for demonstration, but it's easy the transfer the same idea to GraphQL or RPC etc and other languages.

Querying using offset/limit might look something like this:

const results = [];
for (let pageNumber = 0; pageNumber < PAGES_TO_FETCH; pageNumber++) {
    const offset = pageNumber * PAGE_SIZE;
    const requestUrl = `${BASE_URL}pokemon?offset=${offset}&limit=${PAGE_SIZE}`;
    console.log(`Fetching ${requestUrl}`);
    const response = await fetch(requestUrl);
    const resultWrapper = await response.json();
    results.push(...resultWrapper.results);
}

This gives the caller a huge amount of flexibility, including being able to change the page size or jump to any page (more on that layer).

How offset/limit works

Likely you need no explanation of how offset limit works, you simply provide two integers, the first being a starting point and the second being the number of rows to be returned.

What's interesting to discuss is how a database will go about getting these three results: It will be done in two parts, first a scan of offset rows to get to the starting point, and then a scan of limit rows to collect the actual results. As you can imagine in the above example any database system will perform these small scans almost instantly.

We can fairly intuitively reason about how this will scale as well: even in the cases of very large data sets the first few pages will be returned almost instantly as the number of rows that need to be scanned will be very low. However the last page for example, will require scanning over the entire data set.

An oddity we can already notice is for each page the same data will be scanned through the same data again and again.

Some Performance Numbers

In order to demonstrate the performance of an offset/limit approach, a database can be set up with dummy data. PostgreSQL is used in this case however all engines will look relatively similar. This demonstration uses a data set size of 1 million rows to simulate a large (but still reasonable) data set.

The database instance used for testing is running on a dell xps laptop and is not under any load, the only queries being run against it are these test queries.

We can now run through a few scenarios and measure the rough performance. With our million tows and using a reasonable page size of 1000 items we have 1000 pages to play with.

To confirm our reasoning above about the scanning we can run an explain on the page 999 query. We get back the following:

Limit  (cost=18315.67..18334.00 rows=1000 width=37)                       
  ->  Seq Scan on sample_dataset  (cost=0.00..18334.00 rows=1000000 width=37)

Sure enough we're simply scanning 1 million rows to get the results.

Let's put a more "worst-case-scenario" data set to the test. Using the same setup as above but ramping up to 100 million rows.

-- Page 1

select *
from large_sample_dataset 
offset 0
limit 1000

-- 1000 row(s) fetched - 0.002s

-- Page 99999

select *
from large_sample_dataset 
offset 99900000
limit 1000

-- 1000 row(s) fetched - 3s

We're now looking at 3s query times getting the last page on the same unloaded PostgreSQL instance with plenty of grunt.

Initial Performance Takeaways

We can take a few things away from our testing

Postgres can scan really fast

We just scanned one million rows in less than a tenth of a second. In that example we probably don't need to do better than offset/limit.

However we have to imagine that if thousands of users and making these queries concurrently we would see much worse reponse times.

We've also seen that if the data sets are even larger we start to see unreasonable response times.

Offset/limit scales with O(n) complexity

As expected, the more rows we needed to scan, the longer the query took.

The contender: cursors

Limit  (cost=18315.67..18334.00 rows=1000 width=37)

from large_sample_dataset 
offset 0
limit 1000

select *
from large_sample_dataset 
offset 99900000
limit 1000

-- 1000 row(s) fetched - 3s

We can take a few things away from our testing


Postgres can scan really fast

We just scanned one million rows in less than a tenth of a second. In that example we probably don't need to do better than offset/limit.

However we have to imagine that if thousands of users and making these queries concurrently we would see much worse reponse times.

We've also seen that if the data sets are even larger we start to see unreasonable response times.


Offset/limit scales with O(n) complexity

As expected, the more rows we needed to scan, the longer the query took.

posts.html:
I recently completed adding slightly over 10m of LED strips to act as ambient and party lights in one of the rooms of our apartment.

I was left with somewhere around 1m of SK6812 strip and thought about some good use for them. I came up with the idea of a physical status panel about the state of home automations or home lab services etc.

Dashboards are all well and good but there is something more tactile about having panels with blinking lights.

I found https://cdn-learn.adafruit.com/downloads/pdf/neopixels-on-raspberry-pi.pdf which takes you through controller adafruit neopixels with raspberry pi gpio pins.

Housing

Rough Sketch

First Prototypes

It took four prototypes to get something where the strip fit snugly, with the correct spacing and with a reasonable amount of print imperfections on the bridging. These were printed on my Prusa Mk4 with a pretty aggressive speed and with a filament that I don't like and am trying to use up.

First RC

The first release candidate for the housing I printed quite slow in order to get the best results for the bridging, and at the final target size with my preferred filament for labels (Das Filament Tonweiss Matte).

Electronics

The hardware

  • 6LEDs worth (or more) of SK6812
  • A leftover raspberry pi 1 from a draw somewhere
  • USB power for the pi
  • A cheap 5V power supply for the lights
  • 3.3V - 5V level converter

Software

I wanted to try and write as little code as possible for this project. I have a Grist instance setup from a previous project, as well as Node-RED and a Mosquitto instance for MQTT so decided I would try to leverage all these low-code tools as much as possible (obviously for the pi itself I would need to write some minimal code consuming from MQTT and controlling the Neopixels.

No-Code

Embedded
